chapter_title: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle (Wit and Humour)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.activity_title: Stepping into Puddleby: Pre-reading and First Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.43): share thoughts on pets and domestic animals.
Let us read (p.43): imagine communicating with an animal or bird.

time_bands.activity: Open the unit with a quick paired exchange: do you have a pet, and why or why not? After a brief share-out, introduce the story's world — Doctor Dolittle in the English town of Puddleby — and read the opening pages aloud with students following.

Continue the teacher-led read-aloud through the Cat's-food-Man's visit and Polynesia's appearance at the windowsill, pausing at natural story breaks to check vocabulary and keep all students with the text.

Pose the “Let us read” prompt from page 43 about animals and birds that talk: if you could speak to any animal or bird, who would it be and why? Students share briefly in pairs, then one or two pairs report to the class.
Wrap up by asking students to recall one detail from the pages read today that surprised or amused them, and note it in their exercise books as a personal response to the story opening.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's opening unit, so no prior content needs to be named. Watch for students conflating the Cat's-food-Man’s motivation with Dolittle’s own wish — the suggestion comes from outside, and the prose_summary is clear on this. Students who have not encountered a parrot as a speaking character may need a moment to settle into the story's comic tone before the pre-reading discussion takes off.
materials: Blackboard or display for key vocabulary

periods.activity_title: Polynesia Teaches: Comprehension of Part I

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.46): why does the Cat's-food-Man recommend animal doctoring?
Let us discuss (p.46): fill blanks on Dolittle’s reaction to Polynesia’s revelation.
Let us discuss (p.46): predict whether Dolittle will become famous as animal doctor.

time_bands.activity: Having read the opening pages in the previous sitting, briefly recap the Cat's-food-Man’s visit through a whole-class oral retell, then read on from Polynesia’s intervention through to Dolittle’s first lesson in bird language, students following in their textbooks.

Work through the “Let us discuss” MCQ on page 46 about the Cat's-food-Man’s suggestion: students choose individually, then defend their choice in pairs before a class vote and teacher explanation of why the other options are misleading.

Do the fill-in-the-blank task from page 46 on Dolittle’s reaction — “curiosity” and “write” — as a whole-class oral exercise, asking students to point to the lines in the text that confirm each answer.

Close with the open question from page 46: will Dolittle become famous as an animal doctor? Students share a one-sentence prediction with a reason; teacher notes two contrasting views on the board and leaves them for the story to answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the story's premise through the shared read, this unit deepens comprehension of Part I. A common confusion is that students assume Dolittle already knew animal languages before Polynesia revealed them — the prose_summary is explicit that the revelation is new to him, so press students to locate the moment in the text. The open prediction question is genuinely open; accept any reasoned response.

periods.activity_title: The Plough Horse and the Glasses: Reading Part II

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.49): what became a common sight in Puddleby?
Let us think and reflect (p.50): arrange ten story events in correct order.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the second section of the story — the plough horse’s visit, the green spectacles prescription, and the spread of Dolittle’s fame across Puddleby — with students following; pause briefly at the horse’s complaint about the “stupid man over the hill” to invite a quick reaction.

Take up the “Let us discuss” MCQ from page 49 about what became a common sight in Puddleby after Dolittle began treating animals; students select individually, then pairs justify the correct answer — farm animals wearing glasses — by pointing to the relevant paragraph.

Work through the sequencing task from page 50: distribute or display the ten events and, working in pairs, students arrange them in story order; discuss as a class, with the teacher confirming the two pre-filled positions as anchor points.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about Polynesia’s lessons and Dolittle’s first steps into animal medicine, students now encounter the story’s funniest scene. The sequencing task demands close recall of narrative order; watch for students confusing the spread of fame (animals coming from afar) with the earlier local success — the prose_summary marks these as distinct stages. The sequencing task is an in-class pair activity; do not assign it as homework.
materials: Blackboard or printed event strips for sequencing

periods.activity_title: Extract Close Reading: Wit, Empathy, and Satirical Edge

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.50–51): Extract 1 — Polynesia’s bird language reveal.
Let us think and reflect (p.51): Extract 2 — horse’s complaint and Dolittle’s insight.

time_bands.activity: Read Extract 1 from page 50 aloud — the exchange where Polynesia switches to bird language and explains why she never used it with Dolittle before — then ask students to locate the exact lines that answer each sub-question before responding.

Work through the Extract 1 questions from pages 50–51 as a class discussion: the expression “Good Gracious” replaced by “gosh”, Polynesia’s reasoning for withholding bird language, the true/false about her snacking, and Dolittle’s emotional state — each answered with textual evidence before the class agrees.

Read Extract 2 from page 51 aloud — the horse’s request for green spectacles and the story’s satirical conclusion that animal doctoring requires greater cleverness — then take up the extract’s MCQ on Dolittle’s attitude and the fill-in on why doctors take animals for granted.

Invite two or three students to share whether they agree with the extract’s final sentence, briefly giving a personal reason; teacher notes the range of views without resolving it, honouring the story’s gentle satirical openness.

periods.teacher_notes: Having encountered the plough horse’s scene and the story’s comic spread of fame, students are now ready for close textual scrutiny. The ECR sub-question from Extract 2 (“Do you agree?”) is genuinely open — accept any position supported by reasoning; the prose_summary’s final sentence about empathy and communication offers a scaffolding anchor. The analogy fill-in (“ploughing”) may trip students who miss the structural parallel with “digging” — model the analogy pattern before students attempt it.

periods.activity_title: Qualities, Evidence, and Wider Thinking: Final Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.52): questions on Polynesia, Dolittle’s qualities, and viewpoints.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.49): write about challenges Dolittle might face treating more animals.

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the story’s arc — from Polynesia’s lessons to the spread of fame — through a fast whole-class oral recap, then direct students to the five questions on page 52.

Take questions 1 and 2 from page 52 as a guided class discussion: how Polynesia was an effective language teacher (drawing on the Birds’ A.B.C. scene and Jip’s body-language demonstration) and how Dolittle ensured individual attention (separate doors, the tunnel for mice).

Move to questions 3 and 4: students write a short answer (3–4 sentences) on Dolittle’s readiness to follow Polynesia’s advice and then on the qualities that made him famous, citing at least one detail from the text as evidence.

Close with question 5 as a whole-class speculative discussion — what would change if people could suddenly understand animals — accepting imaginative responses; teacher sets the homework challenge from page 49 about challenges Dolittle might face.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through both extracts closely, students now synthesise their understanding of character and theme across the whole story. The most common gap here is vague character description without textual evidence — remind students that the prose_summary explicitly lists the special doors and tunnel as concrete acts of individual care. The open speculation question (question 5) rewards creative thinking; keep discussion brief so the written sub-questions receive adequate time.

periods.activity_title: Clinic Announcement: Critical Listening in Action

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.55): judge true/false about Dr. Dolittle’s clinic announcement.
Let us listen (p.55): complete clinic details with one or two exact words heard.

time_bands.activity: Prepare students for the listening task: explain that they will hear a formal public announcement about Dr. Dolittle’s new clinic in Woodstock, and ask them to hold their pens down during the first reading so they listen without writing.

Read the clinic announcement aloud at a measured pace; students listen and then respond to the true/false question from page 55 (the announcement does not mention free medicines — false) individually in their books.

Read the announcement a second time; students now complete the fill-in task from page 55, writing one or two exact words for each blank — town name, lane name, opening hours, special timings for birds, quality of care, and animal types welcomed.

Take up answers as a class, reading each blank aloud and confirming from the announcement text; discuss briefly what formal announcements typically include and how listening for key details differs from listening for general meaning.

periods.teacher_notes: Having engaged with the story’s world through reading and discussion, students now hear the same fictional world in a formal announcement register. A frequent error is writing paraphrased words rather than exact words from the announcement — press students to use the precise vocabulary they hear. The announcement is on p.88 of the textbook and the teacher reads it aloud; no audio file is required.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.55–56): role-play doctor–patient conversations using four cue cards.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the role-play structure: display or read the four health problems (cough, dry lips, sore throat, fatigue) and their solutions; review the six cue-card steps — greet, enquire, ask symptoms, diagnose, advise, arrange follow-up — with the class.

Pairs take turns as doctor and patient for two of the four problems each; teacher circulates, prompting students who stall at the diagnosis or advice steps and encouraging formal but natural language throughout.

Two pairs demonstrate contrasting problems to the class; teacher and peers offer brief feedback on clarity, appropriate register, and whether the cue-card structure was followed, before closing the activity.

periods.teacher_notes: Having listened to the formal clinic announcement, students now shift to speaking in a doctor–patient register. A common difficulty at this stage is mixing informal and formal registers within the same exchange — remind students that a doctor’s questions and advice use complete sentences and polite phrases. Students who are hesitant should be paired with a supportive peer and given the simpler problems (cough or fatigue) first.
materials: Cue-card prompts (textbook or teacher-prepared on strips)

periods.activity_title: Writing a Notice: Form, Function, and Drafting

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.57): complete the draft notice, then write an original 50-word notice.

time_bands.activity: Teach the notice format explicitly: heading, date, body (who, what, when, where), and contact details; show the word-and-phrase bank from page 57 on the board and briefly explain what each item signals in the notice structure.

Students complete the draft notice by filling in the blanks with the supplied words and phrases from page 57; teacher circulates and checks that the health card detail and assembly hall venue are correctly placed.

Students write their own original notice of about 50 words for the Annual Health Check-up for Grades 6–8, including all required details; peer-read with a partner to check format completeness, then revise before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised oral interaction in the speaking unit, students now move into formal written communication. The most common error in notice writing is omitting the heading or writing the date in an informal format — draw attention to these two features before drafting begins. Both the guided fill-in and the original notice are completed and peer-reviewed within this unit; no draft is carried forward.

periods.activity_title: Compound Words: Three Forms and How They Work

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.52): sort compound words into hyphenated, open, and closed columns.
Let us learn (p.53): match Column A and B to form compounds; complete the paragraph.

time_bands.activity: Draw the three compound-word types from the story on the board — “Cat’s-food-Man” (hyphenated), “bird language” (open), “flowerpots” (closed) — and ask students to say what determines which form is used, accepting any hypothesis before teaching the rule.
Students complete the sorting table from page 52 by placing the seven words from the box into the correct columns; pairs compare answers before whole-class confirmation on the board.

Move to the matching task from page 53: students link Column A and Column B words to form seven compound words, then use their matched words to complete the descriptive paragraph about animals after Dolittle’s treatment.

Quick whole-class review of the completed paragraph, with students reading the sentences aloud and the teacher confirming or correcting the compound selections; note any words that could plausibly combine in more than one way.

periods.teacher_notes: Compound words appear extensively in the story — “plough horse”, “harvest mice”, and “windowsill” are all drawn from the same chapter text, giving students an immediate context. A common error is treating all two-word combinations as open compounds; reinforce that the three types are conventionally fixed, not a matter of preference. Students who finish the paragraph early can be asked to find one more compound word from the story text itself.

periods.activity_title: Hidden Animals, Palindromes, and Tense: Language Patterns

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.53): find hidden animal names embedded in five sentences.
Let us learn (p.54): identify palindrome words and sentences in six examples.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.54): underline verbs and name tense form in four story sentences.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the hidden-animal activity from page 53: read the first sentence aloud and model finding the concealed animal by reading the letters across word boundaries; students then work individually to locate the hidden animals in sentences 2–5, comparing with a partner before class verification.

Introduce palindromes using the story’s example (“never” and “even” from the plough horse’s complaint) as the entry point; read items 1–6 from page 54 aloud and students identify which words or full sentences are palindromes, then share and justify their answers.

Students compose their own palindrome word or sentence and share it with the class; teacher records two or three student creations on the board and confirms their validity by reading forwards and backwards.

Set the homework task from page 54: underline the verbs and name the tense form in the four story sentences; explain the two tense forms — simple present and present continuous — as a brief orientation before students attempt the task independently at home.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised compound-word formation in the previous vocabulary unit, students now explore wordplay embedded in the same chapter text. The hidden-animal task relies on reading across word boundaries — a skill students find genuinely surprising and enjoyable; let them discover rather than being told. The palindrome task draws explicitly on the story (“never”, “even”) which gives it a textual anchor rather than feeling like an isolated puzzle.

periods.activity_title: Present Perfect Tense and Exploring Animal Welfare

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.55): fill six blanks using present perfect tense in a Dolittle paragraph.
Let us explore (p.58): find names of organisations that work for animal welfare.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.58): write a short response on the best way to care for stray animals.

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the two story sentences that introduce the present perfect — “That man’s got sense” and “Can’t you see that it has stopped raining?” — and draw out the form (have/has + past participle) and meaning (action completed with present relevance) from the sentences themselves.

Students complete the six-blank present-perfect fill-in from page 55 about Dolittle’s career; work through the first blank together as a model, then students complete the rest individually before partners check each other’s verb forms.

Transition to the “Let us explore” task from page 58: discuss what animal welfare means in the context of the story, then, working in small groups with whatever reference materials the classroom allows, students list the names of organisations in India that work for animal welfare and share findings.
Set the homework from page 58: students write a short personal response (4–5 sentences) on the best way to care for stray and abandoned animals, choosing one of the three options and giving reasons.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored wordplay and verb tense through the chapter’s language, this unit anchors the present perfect tense firmly in Dolittle’s story rather than in abstract grammar rules. A frequent error is using simple past instead of present perfect (“Dolittle learned” for “Dolittle has learned”) — return to the story sentences to show why the present-relevance meaning demands the perfect form. The animal-welfare research segment works even without internet access if students draw on textbook references to Charaka Samhita and Harita Samhita mentioned in the chapter.
materials: Any available reference on animal welfare organisations

periods.activity_title: Whole-chapter Synthesis: Empathy, Language, and Animal Care

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.58): discuss what a goshala visit would reveal about animal care.

time_bands.activity: Open the synthesis with a whole-class discussion: what single idea connects Polynesia’s language lessons, the plough horse’s spectacles, and the specialised doors Dolittle installed for different species? Draw out the theme of empathy and communication as the foundation of good medicine.

Use the “goshala” context from page 58 as a real-world pivot: students compare how the cows in a traditional goshala are looked after with how Dolittle treats animals in the story, identifying two similarities and one difference in small groups before reporting back.

Students write a short reflective paragraph (6–8 sentences) answering: “What does Doctor Dolittle’s story teach us about listening and empathy, and how do those lessons apply to the way people treat animals today?” — drawing on any part of the story they recall, with no notes or prior draft required.

Three or four students read their paragraphs aloud; teacher draws out one idea from each that connects personal reflection to the story’s satirical point, and closes the chapter by returning to the horse’s wry observation that empathy and communication are the true foundations of medicine.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together the story’s major ideas — Polynesia’s role as a teacher, the plough horse as a patient, and Dolittle’s individualised care — without assuming any particular activity happened in a specific unit. The reflective paragraph is planned, drafted, and completed within this unit; no prior writing is continued or handed back. Students who engage most deeply will connect the story’s gentle satire (the horse’s complaint about ungrateful vets) to contemporary ideas about empathetic practice.

items.item_stem: In the story, the Cat’s-food-Man visits Doctor Dolittle for a stomach-ache and makes a suggestion that changes the doctor’s career. Which of the following best describes what the Cat’s-food-Man believes about Dolittle?

options.label: A
options.text: Dolittle is bored with human medicine and is looking for a change.

options.label: B
options.text: Dolittle understands animals so well that he would make a far better veterinarian.

options.label: C
options.text: Dolittle earns too little treating people and needs to find wealthier patients.

options.label: D
options.text: Dolittle has already learned animal languages from Polynesia.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students choosing this conflate Dolittle’s later willingness to switch with the Cat’s-food-Man’s stated reason, which is about talent, not boredom.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Students choosing this introduce a financial motive that is absent from the text; the Cat’s-food-Man’s reasoning is about competence, not income.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this confuse the sequence of events: Polynesia’s language lessons come after, not before, the Cat’s-food-Man’s visit.

items.item_stem: The plough horse tells Doctor Dolittle that he has been visiting the vet over the hill for weeks but is no better. The horse then says exactly what he needs. Using evidence from the story, explain what the horse’s complaint reveals about how animals are typically treated by doctors, and what Dolittle does differently.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The horse’s complaint reveals that other vets prescribe useless medicines without actually understanding what the animal needs, because animals cannot complain. Dolittle listens to the horse directly, learns it needs green spectacles to shield its eyes while ploughing, and provides exactly that remedy — showing that genuine communication, not guesswork, is the basis of good animal medicine.

items.item_stem: You will hear an announcement about Dr. John Dolittle’s new clinic. Listen carefully and decide whether each statement below is true or false.

options.text: The clinic is located in the town of Woodstock.
The clinic is open on Saturdays for all animals from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Dr. Dolittle is known for his ability to communicate with animals.
Only domestic pets such as cats and dogs are welcome at the clinic.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the announcement states the clinic is in the town of Woodstock.
2. False — Saturday timings (11 a.m. to 2 p.m.) are special timings for birds only, not all animals.
3. True — the announcement explicitly says Dr. Dolittle is renowned for communicating with animals.
4. False — the announcement says all animals are welcome, from horses and cows to pets and wild animals.

items.item_stem: Work with a partner. One of you plays Dr. Dolittle seeing a human patient; the other plays a patient visiting the clinic with a sore throat. expected_elements: Uses a formal greeting and addresses the patient politely.
Asks at least one specific question about symptoms.
States a clear diagnosis and recommends gargling with warm salt water.
Gives at least one piece of additional advice (avoid cold drinks or drink herbal tea).

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Dr. Dolittle and your partner is a patient who is feeling very tired and lacking energy. Without using any written cue cards, have a conversation in which you ask questions to understand the patient’s daily routine, explain what is causing the fatigue, suggest a remedy and additional advice, and give your opinion on why rest and a balanced diet matter. Speak in a polite, formal register throughout.

expected_elements: Asks open questions about the patient’s sleep and diet without reading from notes.
Gives a clear diagnosis naming fatigue and its likely cause.
Recommends adequate sleep, balanced diet, and short walks with a reason.
Maintains formal register and courteous tone throughout the exchange.

items.item_stem: Your school is organising a health check-up for students of Grades 6 to 8. Write a notice of about 50 words to be displayed on the school notice board. Your notice must include: a heading, the purpose of the notice, the date and time, the venue (assembly hall), a reminder about health cards, and how students can contact the school for questions. Use a formal tone and the correct notice format.

expected_elements: Heading clearly labels the notice (e.g., ANNUAL HEALTH CHECK-UP).
Body states date, time, and assembly hall as venue.
Reminds students to collect or carry their health check-up cards.
Includes contact information or name for queries; formal tone maintained.

items.item_stem: Inspired by the story of Doctor Dolittle’s new clinic in Woodstock, imagine that your school is inviting a veterinary doctor to speak to students about animal health and welfare. Write a notice in about 60 words to inform students of Grades 6 to 8 about this special talk. In your notice, explain the purpose of the talk, give the date, time, and venue, say why attending would be valuable, and mention who to contact for further information. Write in your own words using the formal notice format.

expected_elements: Notice has a clear heading and is addressed to the correct audience (Grades 6–8).
States date, time, and venue accurately in the body.
Gives a reason for attending linked to animal health or welfare themes.
Contact detail or issuing authority included; formal notice register maintained throughout.

items.item_stem:
The sentences below are about Doctor Dolittle’s career. Fill in each blank with the correct present-perfect form of the verb in brackets. Then, for sentence 5, explain in one sentence why the present-perfect tense — rather than the simple past — is the right choice.

1. Since opening his animal clinic, Doctor Dolittle ______ (earn) the trust of creatures from across the countryside.
2. Polynesia the parrot ______ (prove) herself a remarkably patient language teacher.
3. Many farm animals ______ (arrive) at Dolittle’s door wearing glasses he prescribed.
4. The news of Dolittle’s skill ______ (spread) to harvest mice, badgers, and bats alike.
5. John Dolittle, M.D., ______ (become) the most celebrated animal doctor in the world.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. has earned; 2. has proved; 3. have arrived; 4. has spread; 5. has become. For sentence 5, the present perfect is correct because Dolittle’s fame began in the past and its result — his ongoing worldwide reputation — still holds true at the time of narration.

items.item_stem: Doctor Dolittle’s story celebrates the idea that animals deserve careful, empathetic care. In India, a traditional institution called the goshala has long provided shelter and care for cows. Research and write a short report (8–10 sentences) in which you: (a) explain what a goshala is and how cows are looked after there; (b) name at least two organisations in India that work for the welfare of animals more broadly; and (c) describe one way in which the values shown in a goshala are similar to the values Doctor Dolittle demonstrates in the story.

expected_elements: Explains goshala as a cow shelter providing food, veterinary care, and refuge.
Names at least two real Indian animal welfare organisations.
Draws an explicit parallel between goshala values and Dolittle’s empathetic practice.
Uses clear, organised sentences with topic-appropriate vocabulary.

items.item_stem: Imagine your neighbourhood has several stray and abandoned animals. Three options are available to help them: (1) leave food and water for them regularly where they live; (2) take them to a registered animal shelter; (3) adopt them and bring them home. Drawing on what the story of Doctor Dolittle teaches about empathy and communication, write a project proposal of 10–12 sentences in which you: recommend the option you consider best, justify your recommendation with at least two reasons, acknowledge one difficulty with your chosen option and how it might be overcome, and explain how Dolittle’s approach to animal care supports your view.

expected_elements: Clearly states one recommended option and gives at least two justified reasons.
Acknowledges a practical difficulty and suggests a realistic solution.
Links the recommendation to Dolittle’s empathy and attentiveness to animal needs.
Proposal is organised, uses formal language, and stays within the theme of animal welfare.
